This vignette shows the functions for summarising and checking regression
models:

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `logist_summary()` | odds ratios, 95% CIs and p-values of a logistic regression |
| `subgroup_effect()` | odds ratios of covariables within each level of an interacting factor |
| `t()` | transposes a `subgroup_effect()` result |
| `as_sstable()` | turns these summaries (or a list of table parts) into an sstable |
| `explicit()` | rewrites a linear model formula with every term spelled out |
| `gg_boxcox()` | Box-Cox profile likelihood plot for a linear model, with `ggplot2` |

```{r}
library(C306)
```

The examples use `baseline_data`, a **simulated** two-arm trial bundled with
the package, so the estimates illustrate the functions and say nothing about
the treatment. We model death (`outcome == 4`):

```{r}
dat <- baseline_data
dat$Arm <- factor(dat$Arm, levels = c("Sham procedure", "Intrathecal treatment"))
dat$sex <- factor(dat$sex, levels = c("F", "M"), labels = c("Female", "Male"))
dat$died <- dat$outcome == 4
```

## Logistic regression: `logist_summary()`

`logist_summary()` takes a fitted binomial `glm` and returns one row per
coefficient with the log odds ratio, odds ratio, 95% CI and p-value.

```{r}
fit <- glm(died ~ Arm + age + sex + apacheii, data = dat, family = binomial)
logist_summary(fit)
```

The default `method = "lik.ratio"` gives profile-likelihood CIs and
likelihood-ratio tests, which behave better than Wald statistics in small
samples or with rare events. `method = "wald"` gives the Wald versions:

```{r}
logist_summary(fit, method = "wald")
```

`stat_digits` and `p_digits` set the decimal places. `verbose = TRUE` prints a
note on the method, and `flextable = TRUE` returns a report-ready table:

```{r}
logist_summary(fit, flextable = TRUE)
```

## Effects within subgroups: `subgroup_effect()`

When a covariable interacts with a factor, its odds ratio differs between the
levels of that factor. `subgroup_effect()` computes the odds ratio, CI and
p-value of each interacting covariable within each level. The factor goes on
the right-hand side of the formula:

```{r}
fit_ia <- glm(died ~ apacheii * Arm + age * Arm, data = dat, family = binomial)
subgroup_effect(~ Arm, fit_ia)
```

Put one covariable on the left-hand side to get a single table with one row
per level:

```{r}
subgroup_effect(apacheii ~ Arm, fit_ia, method = "wald")
```

`t()` regroups the result by covariable instead of by level (the same as
`transpose = TRUE`):

```{r}
t(subgroup_effect(~ Arm, fit_ia, method = "wald"))
```

The model can also be given as a formula, which is then fitted with
`glm(family = binomial)`:

```{r}
subgroup_effect(age ~ Arm, died ~ age * Arm, data = dat, flextable = TRUE)
```

## Converting to sstable: `as_sstable()`

`as_sstable()` converts the result of `logist_summary()` or
`subgroup_effect()` into an sstable (a list with `table` and `footer`), which
the table functions in `vignette("custom-tables", package = "C306")` can
format or combine with other tables:

```{r}
ss <- as_sstable(logist_summary(fit))
ss$table
```

It also assembles a table from parts: a list with `header`, `body` (a named
list of matrices, one per row group) and an optional `footer`.

```{r}
parts <- list(
  header = list(c("", "Sham procedure", "Intrathecal treatment")),
  body = list(
    "Age, years" = rbind(c("Mean", "50.1", "49.8"),
                         c("Median", "51", "49"))
  ),
  footer = "Illustrative numbers."
)
as_sstable(parts, flextable = TRUE)
```

## Explicit model formulas: `explicit()`

In a model with an interaction such as `bmi ~ age * sex`, `drop1()` only
considers dropping the interaction, because the main effects are implied by
it. `explicit()` refits the model with every term written out, so each main
effect can be tested or dropped on its own. The fit itself is unchanged.

```{r}
fit_lm <- lm(bmi ~ age * sex, data = dat)
fit_explicit <- explicit(fit_lm)
formula(fit_explicit)
drop1(fit_explicit)
```

## Box-Cox plot: `gg_boxcox()`

`gg_boxcox()` is a `ggplot2` version of `MASS::boxcox()`. It plots the profile
log-likelihood of the Box-Cox power `lambda` for a linear model with a
positive response, with the 95% confidence interval for `lambda` marked. A
`lambda` near 0 suggests a log transformation, near 1 no transformation.

```{r}
gg_boxcox(icudays ~ Arm + age, data = dat)
```

A fitted `lm` works too, and `lambda` sets the grid:

```{r}
gg_boxcox(lm(icudays ~ Arm + age, data = dat), lambda = seq(-1, 1, 0.05))
```
